Developers urged to create more family-friendly spaces, malls and homes; AC framework updated
article:
Real estate developers and mall owners in Singapore are being called on to provide more family-friendly spaces and amenities in their projects.

Support for marriage and parenthood in Singapore requires a whole-of-society approach, said Indranee Rajah, Second Minister for Finance and National Development, and Minister in the Prime Minister's Office.

Speaking at the Real Estate Developers’ Association of Singapore (Redas) Mid-Autumn Lunch on Sept 23, she noted that the real estate sector — as developers, property owners and landlords, as well as employers — has a meaningful role to play in helping to reverse the downward trend for marriage and parenthood.

Developers have a significant say in how buildings are designed and what features and amenities are provided.

They could thus include intentional and inclusive spaces for families in their projects — whether it be more family-friendly common spaces, lactation rooms or facilities in commercial buildings, and spaces that cater to young children and elderly grandparents alike.

When it comes to malls, Indranee cited feedback from families seeking more common areas where parents can wait for children or seniors, as well as more family-friendly activities.

She urged mall owners to consider their properties as potential community hubs, with activities for singles and families, while encouraging their F&B tenants to adopt more family-friendly features and practices.

At the event, Redas president Tan Swee Yiow similarly highlighted the role developers can play.

Many of the association’s members build the homes that young families move into and the spaces around them, including playgrounds, gardens, communal decks and flexible multigenerational layouts.

"When we get these spaces right, we help families meet their aspirations, whatever shape that family takes," Tan said.

He also floated several ideas for consideration, while clarifying that they are not formal Redas positions.

"For larger developments, perhaps we could allocate a small percentage of units as larger, family-sized homes."

He also suggested exempting gross floor area (GFA) for household shelters so the space could be used to reintroduce helper’s rooms into floor plans, as well as providing more childcare facilities near homes and offices with similar GFA exemptions.

"It takes a village to raise a child. Government, employers, developers and society all have a part to play," Tan said. "We can help more Singaporeans start and grow the families they hope for."

Accredited Checker framework enhanced

Separately, Indranee announced at the event that the government will enhance the Accredited Checker (AC) framework to better support structural design checks.

This is especially for larger, more complex or higher-risk projects.

ACs and ACOs provide independent reviews of structural designs, to ensure the structural integrity of a building and the safety of designs early in the planning stage.

From September 2028, ACs and Accredited Checker Organisations (ACOs) who undertake larger and more complex projects will be required to demonstrate relevant recent checking and design experience, as well as a good track record.

Requirements for smaller and lower-risk projects will be calibrated according to the risks involved, so that individual ACs can continue to take on such projects.

These changes are intended to give developers greater confidence that complex projects are being checked by professionals and organisations with the expertise, personnel and resources required.

Besides, stronger checks upstream will help reduce downstream design issues and rectification costs, Indranee noted.

A two-year transition period will be provided before full implementation in September 2028, and contracts awarded before then will not be affected.

In addition, from 2028 onwards, the Building and Construction Authority will extend the registration and renewal validity for ACs, ACOs and Specialist ACs from 12 months to 36 months to reduce administrative burden.

The Association of Consulting Engineers Singapore has also developed a Value Articulation Framework for AC checking services.

This is meant to give developers and ACs or ACOs a common and transparent basis to discuss the checking approach and resources required for each project. It will help developers assess AC proposals more holistically, based on factors beyond fees alone.

As building works become more complex, it is essential for ACs and ACOs to be equipped with the technical capability, organisational resources and relevant experience to carry out robust and effective checks, Indranee said.

title: $38 mil price tag on Mohamed Sultan Rd commercial, serviced apartment buildings
article:
A freehold mixed-use development with approval for Serviced Apartment (SA1) use has been put on the market with a guide price of about $38 million, or around $2,621 psf on the existing floor area of 14,497 sq ft.

Located at 22 and 23 Mohamed Sultan Road, the assets comprise a serviced apartment block and a commercial building, sitting on separate land parcels with a combined land area of about 4,221 sq ft.

Both are fully tenanted and able to provide stable and immediate rental income to incoming investors, according to exclusive marketing agent CBRE in a Sept 23 media release.

“The assets are well-maintained and in excellent condition, offering a turnkey investment with minimal near-term capital expenditure required,” said Clemence Lee, CBRE executive director of capital markets, Singapore.

Co-living operator Cove is currently managing apartments, lofts and rooms with shared amenities at both properties.

The rear block, at 22 Mohamed Sultan Road, is an eight-storey development approved for SA1 use, housing serviced apartment units on levels two to eight.

It occupies a 3,075 sq ft site zoned for residential use with a gross plot ratio of 3.8 based on the URA Master Plan 2025.

The front block, at 23 Mohamed Sultan Road, is a four-storey building with a basement. It has a shop in the basement, restaurant on the ground floor, and serviced apartments from levels two to four.

That block sits on a land plot spanning 1,146 sq ft, zoned for commercial use.

Online checks show that Bad Habits, which serves New York-style pizzas by the slice, occupies the ground floor of the front block.

Lee noted that such freehold, income-producing mixed-use assets in River Valley are tightly held, while the Singapore River-Robertson Quay district is also undergoing renewal.

The properties are a seven-minute walk to Fort Canning MRT Station and an eight-minute drive to Raffles Place in the CBD and the Orchard Road shopping district.

The sale will be conducted via an expression of interest exercise, which closes at 3pm on Oct 28.

title: Record-smashing $1.701 mil HDB resale: How this Pinnacle@Duxton unit defied the odds
article:
A few years ago, the Lims considered selling their five-room HDB flat at Pinnacle@Duxton. But their property agent, Ink Chua, advised them to hold on to it.

The flat was fetching more than $5,000 a month in rent then, and Chua felt there was no hurry to sell.

This year, she contacted the couple with a different recommendation: It could be a good time to put the flat on the market.

The decision paid off, with the 1,152 sq ft flat recently sold for $1.701 million — setting a new record price at Pinnacle@Duxton.

It exceeded both the previous high of $1.63 million and their initial asking price, by $71,000 and $51,000 respectively.

Before the Lims' sale, the record was held by a five-room unit on the 43rd to 45th floors — sitting far above the couple’s flat on the 28th to 30th storeys — that changed hands in May.

Achieving this record-breaking outcome for their lower-floor, largely unrenovated unit came as a surprise to the Lims.

"We felt shocked, lucky and very grateful. Huat ah !" Mr Lim tells EdgeProp Singapore .

In fact, before putting the flat up for sale, the couple had considered spending a high five-figure sum renovating it to improve its prospects, but Chua advised them against that.

"Ink said not to waste the money and just leave it to her," he notes.

While other units they knew of had been renovated before being sold, the Lims’ flat went on to achieve a record price despite being largely in its original condition.

"We ended up saving quite a bit on renovation, so we're really thankful for Ink," he adds.

'Completely random' beginnings

The Lims' story at Pinnacle@Duxton began more than two decades ago — long before they could have imagined their flat would one day fetch more than $1.7 million.

Situated on Cantonment Road in Tanjong Pagar, the 50-storey Pinnacle@Duxton soars 163m high — currently Singapore's tallest HDB development — and comprises 1,848 units with flexible layouts.

It features an award-winning design by Singapore firm Arc Studio Architecture + Urbanism, with seven HDB blocks linked by sky bridges.

The public housing project was completed in 2009 and has since logged a slew of million-dollar resale deals, including several among the highest-priced HDB flats in Singapore.

The Lims applied for a home at the development in 2004, almost on a whim.

"As the first owners, we didn't exactly choose Pinnacle@Duxton with a grand master plan. We just happened to apply for fun and surprisingly got it," recalls Mr Lim.

“It was all completely random when HDB called us down to select our choice unit.”

They paid about $350,000 to $400,000 for it and collected the keys in 2009.

The couple kept renovations to a minimum and furnished most of the home with movable furniture.

It was their first home together, where they began married life as a young couple in their 20s.

Now aged 40 to 50, the Lims still look back fondly on their years there.

"This home represents our foundational chapters, from early marriage milestones to hosting close friends against the backdrop of the city lights," says Mr Lim.

"It feels very nostalgic, as our younger days were spent in this house."

They also appreciated the convenience of living in the CBD. Mrs Lim recalls being able to get around without driving.

"Having the entire CBD at our doorstep is a luxury, and our favourite feature has always been the sky gardens overlooking the city skyline," she says.

Likewise, her husband remembers the easy commute to work by public transport, as well as the abundance of amenities nearby and the many options for date nights in the city centre.

First home takes on a new role

As their lifestyle needs changed over the years, the Lims eventually left Pinnacle@Duxton.

The couple also wanted to care for and spend more time with their elderly parents, which led them to live together in a landed property owned by the parents. It remains the Lims’ primary residence today.

Living there also gives the Lims, who now have several children, more space as a family.

"It’s in a quiet residential enclave that better suits our lifestyle now," says Mrs Lim.

Meanwhile, they rented out the five-room flat and kept it largely in its original condition.

“That way, whoever buys it next gets a blank canvas and can design it the way they like," says Mrs Lim.

After holding on to the flat for several more years, the Lims decided to take their property agent’s advice to sell this year.

"The market was good and it was the right time to cash out," Mr Lim notes.

They plan to use the proceeds to buy two properties — one for their own stay in the future and another as an investment.

For now, they intend to continue living with their parents.

"It gives us immense comfort… to spend time with our parents and take care of them daily, while they're surrounded by their familiar neighbours and friends," adds Mrs Lim.

Price pushback amid strong interest

Chua, a branch division director at ERA, listed the flat for sale at $1.65 million in June.

The marketing period came with some constraints, as the tenant was overseas for about three weeks and viewings could only take place on weekdays.

She estimates that the flat therefore had about 1.5 months of active viewings within the two to three months it took to secure a buyer.

During that period, the listing attracted close to 30 enquiries and more than 20 viewings, by Chua's estimates. Aside from the eventual buyer, there were roughly eight offers, with some negotiations falling through.

The asking price faced some resistance, as "there was definitely discussion and some strong pushback", Chua says.

Some buyers brought up renovation costs. Others argued for a lower price by pointing to the previous $1.63 million record, which was on a much higher floor at levels 43 to 45.

A few prospective buyers also noted that the view from the flat "was a small pocket of sea view rather than a full panorama", Chua recalls.

"My job was to help them see the bigger picture: five-room flats in the CBD are rare, and there aren’t many available for sale," she continues.

Still, almost everyone liked the spacious interior and central location.

And because the unrenovated interiors made it difficult for some viewers to picture what the home could look like, Chua prepared before-and-after design renderings of possible changes.

“I spoke to each buyer to qualify them and understand their profile and needs… Based on that, I prepared a few variations of the renderings in layout and style," she says.

During viewings, she would walk prospective buyers through the flat and explain how different areas could be reworked.

For example, they may remove a kitchen wall to create an open-concept living and dining area, convert a bedroom into a walk-in wardrobe, or turn a common room into a study with glass sliding doors.

“Because the flat wasn't renovated, I wanted to help potential buyers visualise what their future home could look like and imagine living there. I think it made a big difference," Chua says.

She would also remind viewers that while the interiors could always be tailored to their preferences, the flat's location and size were fixed.

One viewing was all it took

The eventual buyers are a Singaporean couple in their 30s to 40s who are currently living with their parents and purchasing their first property.

According to Chua, they were looking for a well-located home with ample liveable space and convenience.

"They instantly recognised that this unit checked every box," she says. “They viewed the flat just once and loved it immediately."

She adds that the buyers had looked at several alternatives in the market, but the layout efficiency of a five-room Pinnacle@Duxton unit ultimately won them over.

They agreed to fork out $1.701 million — well above the Lims' target price.

The Lims credit Chua’s use of market analytics and people skills with helping to keep the selling process on track.

They say she mapped out the sale strategy using market data while building rapport with prospective buyers.

"As sellers, we did not have to lift a finger to do anything, as we could leave it all to Ink to handle," says Mr Lim with a laugh.

"She made this entire sale a breeze; everything was so, so smooth."

Who is buying at these prices?

Although the buyers of the Lims' flat are first-time homeowners, the approximately 25 viewings drew people at different stages of their property journey.

Among them were other first-time buyers who had been house-hunting for six months to a year.

Some were prepared to pay more for a resale home so they could move in as soon as possible and skip the waiting times for Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

On the other hand, the unit also attracted older buyers who were moving from private homes to public housing.

From Chua's recent transactions, she has similarly observed more private property owners seeking large, well-located HDB flats as their forever homes.

For them, a prime HDB flat can offer lifestyle advantages they value, such as generous space, central location, views and convenience, without having to pay monthly maintenance fees for condo facilities they do not use often.

"In that sense, they might be downgrading in the property category, but certainly not in their day-to-day living experience," she notes.

"With a flat like this [at Pinnacle@Duxton], they can just head downstairs for food and groceries, and everything is nearby."

Chua reckons that more of such buyers will be considering flats like the Lims', given that the government has recently scrapped the 15-month wait-out period for private homeowners purchasing a non-subsidised HDB resale flat without an HDB housing loan.

What buyers prioritise at the million-dollar mark

At the same time, buyers considering million-dollar HDB flats tend to compare them with private condos as well.

The alternatives they evaluate include smaller condo units in the Rest of Central Region and Core Central Region.

“But the mismatch between the price point and actual living space [in some condos] can make it difficult for those planning to start a family. Consequently, many still prefer to purchase a bigger flat that’s ready for immediate occupation," Chua says.

In her experience, buyers of million-dollar HDB flats typically prioritise factors such as the floor level, views, remaining lease and proximity to an MRT station.

Moreover, buyers have become more practical in recent years, placing more weight on the location, unit layout and size.

“They care less about existing renovation because they know they can redo the interiors," Chua says.

"This $1.701 million sale is a good example. Our unit wasn't on the highest floor and didn’t have a full view, but the space and location were strong enough to set a record."

For the Lims, the deal brings to a close more than two decades of ownership that started in 2004.

At the time, they could hardly have known how much that decision would come to shape the years ahead.

Pinnacle@Duxton became their first marital home, followed them through different stages of their lives and later provided a steady stream of rental income.

Now, the home they once acquired largely by chance has given the Lims an unexpected parting gift: a record sale and the means to start planning their next chapter.

title: What Happens to Your Dividends When Interest Rates Stay Higher for Longer?
article:
Interest rates have a major influence on dividend investors, especially following the Federal Reserve’s recent
rate hike
.
The impact differs across sectors: banks can benefit from higher rates, while real estate investment trusts (REITs) typically face headwinds.
But for dividend investors, how do elevated
interest rates
affect your portfolio?
What Does “Higher for Longer” Actually Mean?
“Higher for longer” means central banks keep interest rates elevated to manage inflation.
This increases borrowing costs for households and companies, which can temper corporate investment and consumer spending.
Relatively safer assets like bonds become more competitive as their yields rise.
However, higher interest rates do not automatically mean all dividend stocks will perform poorly.
Companies with low debt, strong cash flow, competitive pricing power, and sustainable payouts remain well-positioned.
The First Impact: Dividend Stocks Face More Competition
When fixed deposits and bonds offer substantially higher returns, a modest 3% dividend yield looks less attractive against equity-market risk.
Investors may rotate between dividend stocks and fixed-income assets as relative returns change.
However, yield alone does not determine an investment’s outcome.
An investor’s total return consists of both dividend income and capital appreciation.
Over a decade, a company offering 3% today while growing its earnings and dividend creates more wealth than a high-yielding company with stagnant growth.
Banks: Higher Rates Can Be a Double-Edged Sword
Banks earn interest on loans while paying interest on deposits and funding.
The difference between these income and funding costs is reflected in the net interest margin (NIM).
If lending rates rise faster than funding costs, NIM expands, supporting earnings and dividends.
However, when rates remain elevated for too long, customers demand higher deposit rates, forcing banks to pay more.
Higher funding costs squeeze NIM, while expensive borrowing weakens loan demand.
For 2Q2026,
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) saw its net interest income (NII) fall 2% year on year (YoY) to S$3.58 billion as interest rates were still lower compared to the prior year.
However, the bank’s balance sheet growth remained strong, with loans rising 8% YoY, led by broad-based lending to large corporates, and deposits increasing 11%.
The Fed’s September 2026 rate hike may reverse this trend.
If rates stay elevated, DBS’s NIM could stabilise or expand, though prolonged high rates still risk squeezing loan demand and raising deposit costs.
REITs: Where Higher Rates Can Hurt the Most
REITs are particularly sensitive to higher interest rates because they use debt to finance property portfolios.
Debt refinancing at higher rates raises expenses, leaving less income available for distribution.
However, not all REITs are equally vulnerable.
Rather than panic
selling
, investors should focus on the REIT’s balance sheet, especially debt-related metrics.
The interest coverage ratio (ICR) will indicate how comfortably operating income covers interest expenses, while REITs with large floating-rate debt exposure feel the strain much faster than those with fixed-rate borrowings.
For example,
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U) (CICT) maintains a moderate gearing of 37.4%, 78% fixed-rate borrowing, an ICR of 3.9x, and an average term to debt maturity of 4.1 years.
While headline yield tells investors what the REIT is distributing today, debt structure provides clues on distribution sustainability.
What Happens to Dividend Payout Ratios?
Higher interest expenses can reduce both earnings and free cash flow, shrinking the cash available for dividends.
Investors should look beyond the headline yield and examine metrics such as free cash flow payout ratio and debt servicing costs.
Free cash flow is particularly important because dividends are ultimately paid with cash, not accounting earnings.
A company might report stable earnings while simultaneously spending more on inventory and debt servicing, reducing the cash available for dividends even when the earnings payout ratio has not changed.
Defensive Dividend Stocks: Do They Hold Up Better?
Certain sectors remain resilient regardless of interest rate movements. Companies supplying essential goods, financial exchanges, or defence systems – such as
Sheng Siong
(SGX: OV8),
Singapore Exchange
(SGX: S68), and
ST Engineering
(SGX: S63) – hold a distinct operational advantage.
The key question is not simply whether a company operates in a “defensive” sector.
Investors should evaluate whether a company can grow revenue enough to offset financing costs by examining revenue resilience, margins, free cash flow, and net debt together.
High-Yield Stocks Can Be Particularly Vulnerable
A
high dividend yield
is attractive, but the highest number does not guarantee the best opportunity.
Ultra-high yields often result from a sharp decline in share price due to deteriorating financial health.
There is an important distinction.
A high yield supported by durable earnings, strong free cash flow, and manageable debt is far more sustainable than one driven by debt or falling stock prices.
Could Higher Rates Actually Create Opportunities?
Higher interest rates can put pressure on valuations across the board, bringing quality dividend stocks down to more attractive valuations.
Additionally, investors with long investment horizons can reinvest dividends at lower share prices to compound future income.
However, one should not buy simply because the dividend yield increased.
The goal is to distinguish between a quality business that has become temporarily cheaper and a business whose financial fundamentals have permanently weakened.
Building a Higher-for-Longer Portfolio
A resilient dividend portfolio combines multiple income sources for diversification, rather than chasing maximum yield.
The portfolio can include:
Income anchors: Companies like DBS Group and Singapore Exchange provide reliable dividends.
Growth income: Companies whose earnings and dividends are still growing, like
iFAST Corporation
(SGX: AIY), even if current yields are modest.
REITs: Quality S-REITs like CICT provide income and property exposure.
Global dividend stocks: Add exposure to different economies and sectors, such as global healthcare with
Pfizer
(NYSE: PFE).
The appropriate mix will depend on an investor’s objectives, risk tolerance, time horizon, and need for current versus future income.
How Should Investors React?
Investors do not need to sell dividend stocks simply because interest rates remain high.
Selling a financially strong company due to short-term price drops means overlooking its long-term value.
Assess your holdings by reviewing the balance sheet, dividend coverage, valuation, and ultimately, the underlying business.
Rebalance where necessary rather than making broad decisions based solely on interest rates.
Get Smart: Look Behind the Yield
Dividend stocks don’t all perform the same during a higher-for-longer interest rate environment.
Banks may benefit from stronger margins, while leveraged REITs and companies may face greater pressure.
Opportunities to buy quality companies at more attractive valuations also emerge in a higher-for-longer environment.
Understanding what supports dividend payouts is ultimately more important than the headline yield.

title: 3 Singapore Stocks That Could Lead the Next Market Rally
article:
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI)’s strong year-to-date (YTD) rally of more than 20% has rewarded investors who stayed invested.
After this first wave of gains, investors tend to start hunting for whatever may lead the next leg – and that’s rarely the stocks that have already run the hardest.
The better candidates are businesses whose earnings could accelerate, valuations still leave room to re-rate, or have catalysts that could shift how the market sees them.
Here are three.
What Could Drive the Next Singapore Market Rally?
Lower interest rates could cut financing costs and support valuations for income-generating assets.
Stronger corporate earnings give any rally a more durable foundation than sentiment alone.
Improving investor sentiment could pull more capital into Singapore equities generally.
And, finally, sector rotation, where money is shifted into laggards with better forward prospects, could also fund the next leg up for the market.
That said, momentum alone won’t be enough; the next leaders need real catalysts behind them.
Seatrium Limited (SGX: 5E2) – The Earnings Growth Leader
Seatrium’s latest numbers for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) show genuine business inflection.
Revenue grew a modest 5% year on year (YoY) to S$5.6 billion, but that’s only part of the story: gross profit rose 22% to S$482 million, and gross margin ticked up to 8.6% from 7.4% a year ago.
The strong follow-through to earnings is best seen in Seatrium’s EBITDA surging 60% to S$651 million and net profit (excluding divestment) jumping 54% to S$212 million.
Seatrium’s return on equity (ROE) was also decent at 7.8%.
The company’s future growth looks bright, with a net order book of S$13.3 billion as of 30 June 2026.
Adding new contracts to this order backlog and continuing the decent showing of expanding profit margins could lead to further earnings growth and a higher share price correspondingly.
To cap things off,
Seatrium
trades at a reasonable forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 15x, against a historical three-year average of 32x.
UOB Group Holdings (SGX: U11) – The Undervalued Blue Chip
Compared to its local bank peers,
DBS
(SGX: D05) and
OCBC
(SGX: O39), UOB’s share price return has trailed.
But UOB currently has a decent valuation with a price-to-book (P/B) ratio of 1.3x, which is the same as the three-year historical average.
Moreover, UOB’s P/B ratio is significantly lower than DBS’ 3.1x and OCBC’s 2.2x.
Despite the valuation discount, UOB has continued to deliver in both earnings and balance sheet strength.
Net profit after tax rose 10% YoY to S$1.5 billion in 1H2026, even though the net interest margin (NIM) declined by 0.17 percentage points to 1.74%.
UOB’s non-performing loans (NPL) ratio is healthy at 1.6%, while it sports a fully phased-in common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 15%.
This affords UOB plenty of room to grow its recent dividend of S$0.88 per share for 1H2026.
Keppel DC REIT (SGX: AJBU) – The Structural Growth Play
Data centre demand tied to AI and cloud computing is about as clean a structural growth trend as exists on the
Singapore Exchange
(SGX: S68).
Keppel DC REIT, or KDC REIT, is Singapore’s largest pure-play vehicle for it, with 25 data centres across 10 countries.
For 1H2026, KDC REIT’s distributable income grew 18.5% YoY to S$150.7 million, and distribution per unit (DPU) rose 11.3% to S$0.05714.
The portfolio’s rental reversion came in around 10%, through renewals in Singapore and Australia, with the weighted average lease to expiry (WALE) extended to 6.7 years from 6.5 years a quarter ago.
Meanwhile, gearing is low at 34%, which gives real financial flexibility to the REIT to acquire more data centres and strengthen its earnings profile.
What Could Stop the Rally?
A global economic slowdown would hit all three, though unevenly.
Higher-for-longer interest rates
would particularly pressure KDC REIT’s valuation and UOB’s re-rating case.
Weakening corporate earnings would undercut Seatrium’s margin story specifically.
Geopolitical uncertainty (already visible in Seatrium’s Middle East-related disruption) is a live risk.
And after a strong run, profit-taking or valuations simply running ahead of fundamentals could stall any of the three regardless of how good the underlying business is.
Should You Buy Before the Next Rally?
Don’t chase what’s already rallied hardest – by definition, less upside remains once expectations are elevated.
Look for earnings before momentum: strong fundamentals are a better foundation than recent price action alone.
Consider staggering purchases rather than deploying all capital at once, since timing any rally precisely is close to impossible.
And keep
valuation
in perspective – even an excellent business can produce poor returns if bought at too high a price.
What Should Investors Monitor From Here?
For all three: quarterly earnings, management guidance, analyst revisions, and valuation changes relative to history.
For Seatrium specifically: new contract wins against that S$32 billion pipeline, and whether margin gains hold once one-off items roll off.
For UOB: The dividend growth, any signs of re-rating in the P/B multiple, and Greater China credit trends.
For KDC REIT: occupancy (watch the Cardiff vacancy that dented 1H2026’s headline number), further acquisitions, and DPU growth sustaining above its historical mid-single-digit pace.

Seatrium, UOB and Keppel DC REIT shouldn’t be judged on how far they’ve already run, but on whether their earnings, cash flows and structural positioning can support another leg higher – and on the evidence so far, all three have a genuine, if different, case.

title: Top 4 S-REITs Raising DPU by 10% or More
article:
Four Singapore
real estate investment trusts
(S-REITs) grew their distribution per unit (DPU) by 10% or more in the first half of 2026 (1H2026).
Naturally, unitholders are wondering whether that same momentum will carry into next year.
The answer largely depends on what is driving each payout.
Not all DPU growth is created equal.
Some increases are locked into long-term lease terms and will repeat for years.
Other gains depend heavily on demand cycles or
currency movements
, meaning they could easily reverse.
What’s powering PLife REIT’s 14.6% DPU growth?
ParkwayLife REIT
(SGX: C2PU), or PLife REIT, owns 73 healthcare properties across Singapore, Japan, and France, with a total portfolio valuation of S$2.56 billion as at 30 June 2026.
Gross revenue dipped 1.6% year on year (YoY) to S$77.1 million for 1H2026, while net property income (NPI) eased 2.0% to S$72.4 million.
A weaker Japanese yen and a tenant exit across five Japan nursing homes dragged down top-line performance.
DPU, however, told a completely different story.
It rose 14.6% YoY to S$0.0877.
The primary driver was the Annual Rent Review Formula for its Singapore hospitals.
Parkway Hospitals Singapore leases all three properties on a triple-net basis through 2042, with committed occupancy holding at a full 100%.
Under the formula, minimum rent jumps 24.3% from S$79.7 million in FY2025 to S$99.1 million in FY2026.
Step-up leases across its France portfolio provided an additional boost.
Furthermore, a tax provision that dragged on 1H2025 results did not recur, making the year-on-year comparison look even more favourable.
Gearing remained healthy at 33.8%.
Can Keppel DC REIT sustain its 11.3% DPU growth?
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU) owns 25 data centres across 10 countries, boasting assets under management of approximately S$6.3 billion.
Gross revenue rose 14.5% YoY to S$242.0 million for 1H2026, while NPI climbed 15.1% to S$210.4 million.
This drove an 11.3% YoY increase in DPU to S$0.05714.
Positive rental reversions of approximately 10% and the newly acquired Tokyo Data Centre 3 were the main catalysts behind the strong growth.
By lettable area, the weighted average lease expiry (WALE) stood comfortably at 6.7 years.
Portfolio occupancy dipped to 92.5% as at 30 June 2026, down from 95.6% a quarter earlier, largely due to the expiration of the Cardiff Data Centre contract in June.
Excluding Cardiff, occupancy would have sat at 95.3%.
Aggregate leverage remained prudent at 34.0%, with average cost of debt coming in at 2.6%.
Market forecasters expect global data centre demand to expand at a 25% compound annual growth rate to 256GW by 2030, offering strong tailwinds.
How did Sasseur REIT grow DPU by 10.2%?
Sasseur REIT
(SGX: CRPU) owns four outlet malls in China valued at S$1.6 billion.
Rather than traditional NPI, the REIT’s income flows through an Entrusted Management Agreement (EMA) tied directly to outlet sales.
EMA rental income rose 6.8% YoY to S$65.4 million in Singapore dollar terms for 1H2026, aided by a stronger Renminbi against the Singapore dollar.
DPU climbed 10.2% to S$0.03366, even after retaining 10% of distributable income.
Record first-half outlet sales of RMB 2.3 billion – up 7.4% YoY – underpinned the performance, supported by a 20.7% surge in shopper traffic to 9.8 million.
Cost of debt also improved, falling to 3.7% from 4.4% at end-2025.
Aggregate leverage stood at 25.6%, making it one of the lowest among S-REITs, while portfolio occupancy held strong at 97.2%.
Because the EMA structure ties income directly to outlet sales, DPU could face pressure if Chinese consumer spending softens or if the RMB weakens against the Singapore dollar.
What’s behind OUE REIT’s 28.6% DPU increase?
OUE REIT (SGX: TS0U) owns office, hospitality and retail properties in Singapore and Sydney, valued at S$6.1 billion.
Revenue rose 3.8% YoY to S$136.1 million for 1H2026, while NPI increased 4.8% to S$110.3 million.
DPU jumped 28.6% YoY to S$0.0126.
Hospitality NPI was a standout, rising 12.3% to S$45.1 million as revenue per available room (RevPAR) climbed 10.7% to S$258.
Meanwhile, finance costs fell 16.6% to S$37.8 million, and joint venture contributions grew 30.6% to S$8.2 million.
OUE REIT also announced the proposed divestment of Crowne Plaza Changi Airport for S$500.0 million.
If completed, unitholders stand to receive S$20 million in special distributions, separate from recurring DPU.
On the risk side, aggregate leverage stood at 41.5% – the highest among the four – and committed occupancy for Singapore offices dropped 3.7 percentage points quarter on quarter to 91.5%.
Get Smart: What kind of DPU growth are you getting?
A headline
DPU growth
rate shows you the immediate reward, but it doesn’t guarantee that the reward will recur.
PLife REIT’s contractual rent review formula runs all the way to 2042, making its distribution growth the most predictable of the group.
The other three REITs rely on operational execution, retail sales, or hospitality demand – variables that can easily shift.
Every growth driver comes with a different shelf life.
Whenever you spot double-digit DPU growth, look beyond the main number.
Always ask what is driving the raise – and whether it actually has staying power.

title: AEM Holdings Has Delivered 443%+ Returns YTD: What’s Next?
article:
AEM Holdings
(SGX: AWX) delivered a total return of over 443% year to date as of last Friday (18 September 2026), according to Fiscal.ai.
AEM makes test handlers and systems for the semiconductor industry.
A return of 443% in under nine months is eye-catching.
The company’s first-half results provide reasons why the stock is gaining.
What drove AEM’s first-half performance?
Revenue rose 29.9% year on year to S$247.2 million for the first half of 2026 (1H 2026).
Net profit hit S$31 million, a 10-fold increase from S$3.1 million a year ago.
The margin expansion is worth highlighting.
Gross margin rose from 25.4% to 33.1% on a better segment mix, leading to net margin reaching 12.5%, up from 1.6% in 1H 2025.
Test Cell Solutions drove the results.
Revenue from this segment grew 52.5% year on year to S$180.9 million, around 73% of group revenue.
A single fabless AI and high-performance computing (HPC) customer became AEM’s top revenue contributor for the half.
This is a meaningful shift.
The message?
AEM’s revenue base is broadening beyond its traditional PC/Foundry customer.
This is an important development, as the business is becoming less concentrated and
more diversified
.
The dividend reward
AEM last declared an
interim dividend
in 1H 2022.
Four years on, it paid S$0.024 per share for 1H 2026.
Management could have stuck with a once-a-year final dividend.
It chose to bring back the interim.
That tells you it expects to keep paying.
Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to S$630 million to S$680 million, up from S$550 million to S$600 million.
AEM attributed the increase to its fabless AI/HPC ramp and its PC/Foundry customer’s adoption of the Asynchronous Modular Parallel Smart (AMPS) platform.
For the first time, AEM also guided towards earnings per share of between S$0.245 and S$0.275.
Where does AEM’s growth go from here?
AEM has built its strategy around five business pillars.
Source: AEM’s 1H 2026 earnings presentation
Two are already contributing to revenue and margins.
Three are still in development.
Pillar 01 centres on its PC/Foundry customer.
AEM does not name this customer, but it is widely presumed to be
Intel
(NASDAQ: INTC).
The semiconductor equipment maker plans to expand the installed fleet through Test 1.5 upgrades.
The harder future insertions would go to Test 2.0.
It’s worth decoding these labels.
Think of the configurables and collaterals under Test 1.5 as the razor blades.
The full systems and handlers under Test 2.0 are the razors.
AEM is building a razor-and-razor blade business.
Pillar 02 targets its PC/AI fabless customer.
Most analysts point to
Advanced Micro Devices
(NASDAQ: AMD) as the likely name.
AEM aims to sustain the high-volume ramp and gradually shift more demanding insertions onto its own solutions.
The semiconductor firm credits these two pillars for its raised 2026 guidance.
The company’s order backlog for the AMPS platform now exceeds S$400 million, and both the AI/HPC fabless and PC/Foundry customers continue to add orders.
The remaining three pillars still need to prove themselves.
Pillar 03 (Memory) requires AEM to qualify its Xact handler at its first memory integrated device manufacturer (IDM).
The ramp is pencilled in for 2027.
This would mark AEM’s entry into the memory testing market.
Pillar 04 taps on outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies (OSATs) and runs through
ASE Technology
(NYSE: ASX).
AEM’s approach is to track the chiplet as it moves through AI/HPC OSATs.
The channel gives AEM a path to hyperscalers it could not have reached alone.
Pillar 05 (Contract Manufacturing) aims to support AEM’s semiconductor ramp and lift its own profitability.
What about the cash flow?
Income investors
, though, have their eyes on AEM’s free cash flow.
And for good reason.
AEM’s free cash flow fell to just S$2 million in 1H 2026, down from S$37.4 million a year ago.
Operating cash flow dropped to S$12.5 million from S$46.4 million a year ago.
Where did the cash go?
Inventories consumed S$37.6 million and receivables another S$31.5 million.
Management says the inventory build supports second-half growth.
AEM has S$80 million in net cash to cover its dividend obligations.
Get Smart: Priced for the future, not the past
AEM grew net profit 10-fold in 1H 2026.
But its free cash flow fell to S$2 million.
Profit without cash flow is a promise, not proof.
To be fair, the future looks promising.
Two of AEM’s five pillars are delivering, and the AMPS backlog tops S$400 million.
For investors looking for dividends, the milestone to watch is whether AEM can convert profits into cash.
With more cash, the chances of higher dividends rise.

title: Bitcoin ETF flows turn positive after US$4.6 bil rebound
article:
(Sept 23): Flows into US-listed spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds have swung positive for the year as a recovery in the largest cryptocurrency revives investor demand.

The cohort has taken in about US$320 million on a net basis in 2026, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Investors have poured roughly US$4.6 billion into the funds since Aug 19, when the US Treasury said it would increase buybacks of long-dated bonds, reversing outflows accumulated earlier in the year.

Bitcoin has rallied about 35% in that period to above US$86,000, finally breaking out of a slump that had kept it mostly below US$80,000 since February. The token was trading around US$85,900 early Wednesday morning in New York.

Digital assets have also climbed back to US$3 trillion in total market value for the first time since January, according to CoinGecko data.

The rally has been accompanied by a pickup in leverage. Open interest in perpetual futures across cryptocurrencies has climbed to about US$160 billion, the highest since late October last year, according to Coinglass data.

See also: Bitcoin retreats from eight-month high after dizzying 13% rally

The renewed ETF demand marks a shift from earlier in the year, when persistent redemptions weighed on the funds while bitcoin was under pressure.

The average holder of US spot bitcoin ETFs “is now comfortably back in unrealised profit”, according to Chris Weston, head of research at the brokerage Pepperstone. He estimated the average cost of bitcoin held by the funds at US$82,000.

“Having endured a meaningful drawdown, I don’t necessarily see the move back above aggregate break-even as an obvious trigger to take profit,” he wrote in a note.

See also: US DOJ probing Binance over potential Iran sanctions violations — Bloomberg

Paul Howard, senior director at the trading firm Wincent, said the rally has caught many by surprise, with attention largely on developments in artificial intelligence this year.

“The move increasingly looks sustainable, with ETF flows providing support around the US$80,000 to US$85,000 range,” he said. “The strength of the move brings the widely discussed US$100,000 year-end bitcoin target increasingly into range.”

title: EU answer to US banking deregulation triggers political pushback
article:
(Sept 23): Brussels is facing pressure to reassess its approach to its landmark banking competitiveness proposal, amid fresh political calls for the bloc to prioritise some elements of the package.

Germany has been privately pushing for the proposal to be split — an idea rejected by EU Financial Services Commissioner Maria Luis Albuquerque last week — according to people familiar with the matter. Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis is also in favour of dividing the plan by advancing work on reforms designed to cut red tape while postponing other more controversial elements such as a pan-European deposit insurance framework to a later date, people familiar with the matter said.

The dissent risks sparking divisions within the EU about how to move forward with its landmark banking package, which was unveiled by the European Commission, the EU’s executive branch, in July.

The initiative aims to revamp the EU’s banking system by reducing national barriers for pan-European banks as well as simplifying some parts of the capital structure and improving regulatory treatments for activities like trade finance. It comes as European lenders fear they are at a disadvantage compared to Wall Street rivals, which are riding high on a wave of deregulation in the US.

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil proposed a two-tier approach during a meeting of EU finance ministers last weekend, advocating that issues such as simplification should come first and more complex issues discussed in parallel, the people said.

That position is shared by Dombrovskis, the EU’s economy commissioner, according to people familiar with the matter, potentially setting up a clash within the EU’s executive arm about how best to progress the legislation. Dombrovskis, who is spearheading the commission’s efforts to cut red tape across different EU legislation, wants to split the package to concentrate on cutting bureaucracy first.

See also: BOE officials leave London for Leeds to set interest rates

The calls to split the package put Germany and the EU’s top economy official in the same camp as the region’s banks, who have similarly called for a staggered approach.

Germany’s finance ministry told Bloomberg News that the country advocates giving “priority” to measures that “directly contribute to the goal of competitiveness and drive investment.”

“Experience has shown that structural issues related to the single market and the banking union are more complex,” the ministry added.

See also: Phillip Nova opens trading joint venture in Uzbekistan

Germany has long opposed a European Deposit Insurance Scheme, which was first proposed in 2015 as part of the nascent banking union. While the EU ultimately agreed on a common resolution and supervision system for banks in the region, the pan-European deposit insurance idea remained stalled as some countries feared that their national deposit guarantee schemes could be used to bail out banks in other economies.

The latest calls for changes to the commission’s new banking proposal follow significant industry pushback.

Europe’s most powerful banks have been collectively leading a call to split up the package as they fear that wrangling over the deposit plan will jeopardise the entire package ahead of a slate of European elections next year.

Bloomberg reported on Tuesday that Europe’s biggest banks and lobbying groups are contesting key parts of a plan by the EU to revive the fortunes of the bloc’s financial system.

Lenders, lobbies and others submitted 121 responses to the European Commission, including calls for some elements to be dropped, fresh ones to be introduced and demands for swifter action.

The consultation feedback, sent by the Sept 15 deadline, highlights the complex path ahead for a package seen as vital to boosting Europe’s economic growth and financial sovereignty. Both the European Parliament and EU countries need to approve the proposal.

title: SoftBank-backed Carro said to mull first dual Nasdaq-SGX IPO
article:
(Sept 23): Used-car marketplace Carro is considering offering shares on Singapore Exchange Ltd’s Global Listing Board, people familiar with the matter said, potentially positioning it to be the first company to use the new dual-listing mechanism with Nasdaq Inc.

Carro has filed confidentially for an initial public offering in the US and recently submitted paperwork for a Singapore listing as well, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public.

The Singapore-based company, which is backed by SoftBank Group Corp, could raise as much as US$400 million ($511.1 billion) to US$500 million, the people said. It’s targeting a dual listing later this year or first half of next year, the people said.

Deliberations are ongoing and details of the potential offering could change, according to the people. Carro could also decide against a Singapore listing depending on investor demand, they said.

“The company considers and evaluates potential financing needs and opportunities from time to time and will make disclosures when appropriate to do so,” a spokesperson for Carro said in an emailed statement.

Carro’s move is a boon for Singapore as it seeks to improve liquidity and broaden its base of publicly traded companies. Under the dual-listing system, which was first announced last year, companies need only prepare a single set of documents to float simultaneously in the US and Singapore, and the timing of their debuts will be aligned. Requirements include having at least S$2 billion in market value.

See also: Nvidia-backed AI startup seeks US$10 billion before Australian IPO

VenueDayOne Data Centers Ltd had also previously been considering a listing on SGX’s Global Listing Board that could have made it the first to use the new mechanism. The company has now decided not to pursue a concurrent dual listing and will instead focus on its US IPO for now, according to people familiar with the situation.

DayOne confidentially filed for a US IPO in August and could raise US$5 billion, Bloomberg News has reported. It may still look to list in Singapore later, the people said.

See also: BlackRock said to buy into GCash owner IPO priced below maximum

Singapore hasn’t hosted a listing of US$1 billion or more since 2018, when Korean internet company Kakao Corp sold global depositary shares, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. IPOs in the city-state have fetched about US$1.1 billion this year, a 33% increase from the same period in 2025. While that’s an improvement, largely thanks to UI Boustead REIT’s offering, it’s a fraction of the proceeds in Hong Kong and India, which have raised about US$48 billion and US$11 billion, respectively.

In other market initiatives, Singapore has also set aside S$5 billion to be allocated to selected fund managers to invest in local stocks.

title: Keppel REIT to divest T Tower at agreed property value of 348.8 bil won
article:
Keppel REIT will divest its 99.38% interest in T Tower in Seoul at an agreed property value of 348.8 billion won ($326.6 million). Keppel Capital Investment Holdings Pte. Ltd., which holds the remaining 0.62% interest in the property, will also divest its stake.

The sum represents a premium of 37.2% to the property’s purchase price when it was acquired in May 2019 and a 7.4% premium to its valuation as at Aug 31 in local currency terms. Keppel REIT announced that it was acquiring the 28-storey freehold Grade A office building at an agreed property value of 252.6 billion won or $301.4 million at the time. Completed in 2010, the property has a gross floor area of 41,598 sq m and attributable net lettable area of 21,084 sq m. It was 92.1% occupied as at June 30.

Based on the REIT’s net property income (NPI) of $12.1 million for FY2025, the transaction reflects an exit NPI yield of 3.9%.

“The proposed divestment of T Tower demonstrates the manager’s disciplined approach to portfolio optimisation and capital allocation. The divestment of the property at an attractive premium to both its acquisition price and valuation demonstrates Keppel REIT’s ability to crystallise value,” says Chua Hsien Yang, CEO of the REIT manager.

“Together with the recent divestment of KR Ginza II in Tokyo, the transaction underscores our strategic capital recycling capability, strengthens Keppel REIT’s balance sheet and enhances the REIT’s financial flexibility,” he adds. The REIT announced the divestment of the freehold boutique office building in Tokyo in July and completed the divestment in August.

Following the divestments, Singapore will account of 81.1% of the REIT’s portfolio value, Chua points out.

See also: MLT to divest property in Shanghai, China for RMB323 mil, extends lease at 201 Keppel Road for another nine months

In its Sept 23 statement, Keppel REIT says it intends to use up to $25 million from the net sale proceeds to conduct unit buybacks on the open market following its 3QFY2026 business update.

That said, should the net sale proceeds be fully used to pare off debt, the REIT says its aggregate leverage post-divestment will improve to 38% from 40% as at June 30 on a pro forma basis.

The divestment is expected to be completed in 4Q2026.

Units in Keppel REIT closed 1 cent higher or 1.18% up at 86 cents on Sept 23.

title: BOE officials leave London for Leeds to set interest rates
article:
(Sept 23): Barring remote sessions during Covid-19, the UK’s rate setters have gathered in London to make their decision at every meeting since the Bank of England gained independence over monetary policy. From next year, the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street will split the duty with Leeds.

In keeping with the prevailing political mood, the Monetary Policy Committee’s nine members will travel north to the BOE’s offices in the West Yorkshire city to thrash out their rate decision, inaugurating a new phase in the bank’s 332-year history. The first MPC meeting in the north may come as soon as December but is more likely to coincide with the March 18 vote next year, according to a person with knowledge of the discussions.

The decision for the MPC to make the symbolic journey coincides with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s push to focus on the north of England, including the creation of the Number 10 North office in Manchester, where he was mayor for almost a decade. But the central bank has had a long association with Leeds, having first opened a branch there in 1827.

In 2021, when Burnham was still a twinkling in the eye of the broader UK electorate, the bank announced plans for a northern hub and moved to a larger office two years later with a goal of growing the team to 500 by 2027. Earlier this week, the BOE said it would be shifting to a new office at Capitol House in Bond Court from 2028 as it presses ahead with plans to have one in 10 of its staff based in the city.

Under the plans, the MPC will meet in Leeds only for decisions that are not accompanied by a full economic forecast, which involve more presentations by staff in the London office. The MPC has eight meetings a year, four of which come with new forecasts.

MPC members regularly travel across the country to learn what is happening in the economy from businesses and contacts, bolstering what they learn from the bank’s network of regional agents. But interest rate decisions have so far been reserved for the committee room in the bank’s listed building in the City of London.

See also: Phillip Nova opens trading joint venture in Uzbekistan

Announcing the new office this week, BOE Governor Andrew Bailey said it was “an important milestone in our long-term commitment to the city”. Tracy Brabin, Labour’s mayor of West Yorkshire, said the decision was “a powerful endorsement of our Northern Square Mile and signals a national belief in our region’s economic future”.

title: Xi unlikely to bring CEOs to summit where Trump seeks deals
article:
(Sept 23): The highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping will bring together a robust gathering of US corporate leaders, but there will not be a comparable delegation of Chinese executives, raising questions about the prospects for the world’s two largest economies to strike new business deals this week.

The Chinese president is not expected to bring any chief executive officers to the US as part of a business delegation, according to a senior US administration official, who sought anonymity to discuss details that are not yet public.

Trump is preparing to host Xi in Washington, with talks set for Thursday and a lavish state dinner, at which many prominent technology executives are expected to attend. Trump told reporters last week that he expected to notch “a lot of different deals” during the summit.

On the US side, tech executives expected to attend the dinner include Meta Platforms Inc’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia Corp’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Microsoft Corp’s Satya Nadella, Amazon.com Inc’s Jeff Bezos, Apple Inc’s Tim Cook, Tesla Inc’s Elon Musk, Alphabet Inc’s Sundar Pichai and Michael Dell of Dell Technologies Inc. They are set to be joined by Jane Fraser of Citigroup Inc and Jamie Dimon of JPMorgan Chase & Co. Mastercard Inc CEO Michael Miebach is also expected to attend.

Others participating in the summit include Trump officials on the forefront of his economic and trade agenda, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, among others, according to a person familiar with the matter.

While the plans and attendees are subject to change, the lopsided list of executives on the American side reflects a potential difference in expectations between the two countries. Trump has repeatedly expressed his anticipation for the summit, calling the Xi visit a “great honour” and highlighting his rapport with the Chinese leader.

See also: Global inflation will linger and Fed will hike rates again, OECD says

The meeting comes at a politically difficult time for Trump, whose party faces midterm elections in November that could mean the loss of one or both houses of Congress and hinder the president’s agenda over the next two years. Xi is approaching an expected fourth term in office amid a slowing economy.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that Xi would be unlikely to bring a group of executives with him to Washington.

During a state visit to the US in 2015, Xi brought a sizeable business contingent, including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s Jack Ma, Tencent Holdings Ltd’s Pony Ma and executives from Chinese state-owned companies.

See also: Hong Kong’s Paul Chan rejects ‘race to bottom’ with Singapore

In the runup to the summit, tensions have grown between Washington and Beijing over artificial intelligence, critical mineral exports and Taiwan, among other issues. Earlier this week, Greer indicated to Bloomberg Television that the US and China were still divided on the terms of a trade truce extension.

Part of the consideration for the delegation’s size could be space-related. Trump, who has for months complained about the limited space in the White House to host large events, has defended plans to construct a massive ballroom on the grounds by saying it was needed to host gatherings such as the state dinner with Xi.

title: SoftBank offers record yields on jumbo junk bonds in AI push — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 23): Billionaire Masayoshi Son’s SoftBank Group Corp kicked off what’s set to be one of the largest corporate junk bond sales ever as the Japanese conglomerate offers record yields to entice investors into helping fund its unprecedented investments in artificial intelligence (AI).

One of the world’s biggest investors in AI, SoftBank started marketing the multi-part deal, with price talk underway, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified as the discussions are private. The group aims to raise the equivalent of more than US$11 billion ($14.03 billion) in the offering that includes a US$10 billion dollar part and a €1 billion (US$1.1 billion or $1.46 billion) euro portion.

The deal is the latest in a flurry of activity by SoftBank in debt markets this year to help fund commitments nearing US$65 billion to ChatGPT creator OpenAI, as well as more M&A in the sector. The moves have put the Japanese investment firm at the epicentre of debt-fuelled bets on artificial intelligence, at a time when the promise of the technology has riveted global markets even as safety concerns about the industry have flared.

SoftBank is offering record yields in the junk debt sale, though those figures could change by the time the deal actually prices.

The conglomerate is marketing US$1 billion of 3.5-year bonds to yield 8.75% to 8.875%, US$4.5 billion of 5.5-year securities at 9.375% to 9.5% and the same amount of 7.5-year notes at 9.75% to 9.875%, the person said. Those would be the highest-ever levels for SoftBank dollar bonds of those maturities, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

See also: Alibaba to add data centres in Europe, Middle East in AI push

As of late afternoon Wednesday in Asia, the order book for the dollar part of the deal had exceeded US$30 billion, people familiar with the matter said.

For the euro portion, SoftBank is marketing four-year notes at a yield of around 7.5%, and six-year securities at 8.25% to 8.5%. That would be at or near a record for the first part and a record for the longer tranche.

The group isn’t alone in storming markets for funding, with global AI-related debt issuance already topping US$575 billion in 2026, according to a recent report by Goldman Sachs Group Inc credit strategists.

See also: China’s AI trade favours global winners over local champions

Son has downplayed concerns about investments in AI infrastructure, and said earlier this year he expects AI-related industries to account for 20% of global output by 2040, equivalent to US$46 trillion.

The flood of AI funding in global financial markets, however, has made some bond investors uneasy. Their concern is that the ever-growing pile of the debt threatens to cause a hangover for markets if the technology fails to pay off for the firms that are making the biggest investments.

With price talk for the shortest SoftBank tranche of 3.5 years starting at 8.75% to 8.875%, if the company ended up paying within that range it would be closer to the average market yield of 8.5% on B- rated notes in the US market, several levels below the Japanese company’s own rating of BB+, the highest speculative-grade score from S&P, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Broadly, the average yield on dollar bonds rated in the B zone is 7.5% and 6.55% for those rated in the BB area, Bloomberg indices show.

title: SGX RegCo rolls out enhanced disclosures to drive value creation
article:
The Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) is rolling out new rules to require enhanced disclosures among listed issuers on their remuneration, dividend policies, and investor relations.

The new rules, which take effect on Jan 1, 2027, come just months after SGX RegCo wrapped up a public consultation to obtain feedback on the new requirements. The exercise, which ran from April 22 to May 22, drew comments from 32 respondents, including asset managers, service providers, representative bodies, issuers and market professionals.

“The rule changes strengthen disclosure standards while preserving flexibility for issuers,” says SGX RegCo CEO Tan Boon Gin. “We encourage issuers to look beyond the minimum requirements, and to provide substantive and meaningful disclosures, such that they can attract global capital and improve valuations.”

Based on the new rules, annual reports for financial years commencing on or after Jan 1, 2027 must describe the key financial and non-financial indicators a listed issuer is using to determine the remuneration of its executive directors and executive officers. In addition, the reports must explain how these indicators are aligned with long-term value creation objectives.

Listed issuers will have to include their dividend policy, investor relations policy as well as a description of any key shareholder engagement activities they are organising within the year.

Notably, SGX RegCo is not expecting issuers to commit to a dividend payout when disclosing their dividend policy. Issuers who wish to retain capital for growth can say so in their policies.

See also: EQDP fund manager Eastspring Investments launches new Singapore Income and Growth Equity Fund

Listed issuers are now required to include investor engagement channels that shareholders can use to contact them as part of their investor relations policy. Starting next year, all issuers must either have a website for investor engagement or a dedicated section on their main website for investor engagement.

Issuers are to include on the website their investor relations policy, annual general meeting minutes, investor presentation decks as well as a calendar of upcoming events. The website is meant to complement SGXNET, which will remain the primary channel for the dissemination of information, SGX RegCo says.

SGX RegCo says the first batch of annual reports that are required to comply with the new rules will be issued from 2028 onwards, although early adoption is encouraged.

See also: SGX to implement post-trade custody model from mid-July; lower board lot sizes in early October

According to annual reports compiled by SGX RegCo for FY2025, more than 90% of issuers incorporate financial indicators in their remuneration frameworks, but only 47% of issuers disclose the indicators used.

More than 90% of issuers maintain a website for investor engagement and have established a two-way communication channel for shareholders, SGX RegCo notes. 80% of issuers disclose the objectives and principles of their investor relations policies, but only a minority give details about their shareholder engagement activities.

“Singapore’s equity market is benefiting from a resurgence of investor interest, but this interest will not last if boards and management do not increase investor engagement and demonstrate greater transparency – particularly transparency about how board or management decisions align with shareholder interests,” Tan says.

title: Trump and Xi seek safe AI without slowing the race for supremacy
article:
(Sept 23): Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, will sit down this week to hash out a plethora of thorny issues from trade to Taiwan. One thing both sides agree on: neither can afford to tap the brakes on artificial intelligence (AI).

While Silicon Valley debates the possibility of AI wiping out humanity, Washington and Beijing appear more worried about global technological supremacy. The two countries have signalled no intention to slow down AI development — a debate that flared anew after Anthropic PBC co-founder Dario Amodei warned of the dangers of unbridled progress in a 3,800-word communique.

Trump almost immediately dismissed calls for moderation as a “hoax” and vowed to maintain American leadership. Beijing sees little reason to slow down in part because it’s already behind the US in AI — though closing the gap — and constrained by American curbs on access to advanced chips by Nvidia Corp.

Just two days before Trump’s set to personally greet Xi at a military airbase, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd declared it was building a mega model of up to 10 trillion parameters, rolling out AI chips it called China’s most powerful, and planning a 20-gigawatt data centre buildout that could translate into US$160 billion ($204 billion) of cloud revenue, by one estimate.

That capped a frenetic few days for Chinese AI, with Z.AI Co and Xiaomi Corp showcasing how their AI systems improve themselves, and Huawei Technologies Co accelerating the debut of high-powered AI chips intended to replace Nvidia’s processors. Manus — the agentic AI pioneer finally clear of Meta Platforms Inc — sought to raise capital at a US$4 billion valuation to bankroll its next act.

“Neither side wants to give up the development or slow down the development,” said Elly Rostoum, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis and a former US intelligence analyst. “But they understand that this is serious enough that they have to talk, that the companies have to talk.”

See also: Sea to adopt Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform; more Southeast Asian firms build with Nemotron

The shared desire by the US and China to push forward suggests Thursday’s summit is more likely to produce narrowly defined guardrails rather than speed limits on AI, even as they take tentative steps to build consensus around critical risks. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington proposed an emergency hotline for AI incidents and discussed a dialogue mechanism with his Chinese counterparts at a Sunday meeting in New York.

“China already sees itself as being forced to pace because of US tech containment and chip export controls,” Selina Xu, who leads China and AI policy research in the office of former Google chief Eric Schmidt, said in an online post. “One remark I have heard from Chinese policymakers is ‘we are already being slowed down.’”

See also: Singapore wants AI to shop but with strict limits, study shows

To close the gap with the US, China has seized on open-weight AI as a strategy to catch up at home and expand its influence abroad. Beijing is keen to keep up that momentum.

Breakout models such as DeepSeek’s R1 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 can be downloaded and adapted by developers worldwide, allowing Chinese laboratories to build on one another’s work and squeeze more performance from limited computing resources. This has also won fans overseas and helped embed Chinese software in workflows and products, paving the way for monetisation.

Moonshot, for example, is building a team of specialised engineers to help clients deploy and customise models, starting in China before expanding globally. It’s also entering commercial partnerships with American cloud providers like Fireworks AI and Baseten to host them.

Z.ai has helped Malaysia build sovereign AI infrastructure, while Saudi Arabia’s state-backed Humain commissioned MiniMax Group Inc to build a national platform based on one of the Chinese start-up’s open models.

Their popularity — a combination of cost, flexibility and performance — has threatened the ability of leading US AI labs to charge for access to their proprietary offerings. Anthropic and OpenAI have both alleged that Chinese companies use the output from their frontier models to create rival systems at a fraction of the cost, a process known as distillation.

The MiniMax deal drew immediate backlash from US national security hawks. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote on X that Washington was “getting played” after agreeing to sell AI chips to Middle Eastern nations on the promise they would rely on an American software stack — only for Saudi Arabia to adopt Chinese technology.

The risk is that these allegations, which Bessent and other officials have echoed, could lead to tougher enforcement of export controls to starve China of the computing resources required to keep up.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The focus on AI risks suggests a shift in emphasis for a rivalry long dominated by US limits on China’s access to advanced chips. Export controls remain a major source of tension and may still emerge during Xi’s visit, but they have received less attention in the days before his arrival.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said export controls were not on the agenda at his Sunday meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and chief trade negotiator Li Chenggang. Beijing hasn’t confirmed the US account of the exchange, saying only that the two sides discussed AI.

China’s continued grip on the global supply of critical minerals likely gives Xi crucial leverage, while Chinese companies including Alibaba accelerate efforts to produce advanced chips that would make the country less vulnerable to Washington’s curbs.

But China is not dismissing the technology’s dangers altogether. Since ChatGPT’s debut in 2022, regulators have introduced rules governing chatbots and proposed restrictions on virtual companions for children. Security officials have also warned about threats of the tools being abused by third parties. This week, The Information reported that China’s cyberspace regulators were investigating potential data breaches by Moonshot and DeepSeek, underscoring Beijing’s intent to police the industry especially around sensitive content.

Those concerns offer potential common ground with the Trump administration, even if they don’t align with the grave risks identified by Amodei and seconded by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk.

“The existential risk from AI is really not a major topic in China, and not a major topic in the Chinese policymaking world,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow with the Brookings Institution. “There’s growing convergence in some of the concerns around other major AI risks, namely around cybersecurity, biological weapons, non-state actors.”

But any agreement on those areas will have to overcome profound distrust about whether the other side is genuinely addressing safety or merely seeking an advantage.

Amodei has argued that preventing China from gaining an AI edge is paramount for safety, a position he’s used to justify tougher export controls. Beijing sees that logic as evidence that calls for safety can serve as a rationale for containment, calling it “fearmongering”.

“Cooperation remains limited for the two countries due to low level of trust,” said George Chen, a partner at consultancy The Asia Group. Beijing continues to believe Washington is seeking to suppress China’s rise in AI and other emerging technologies, a perception that will shape the pace and scope of future engagement, he said.

title: Global inflation will linger and Fed will hike rates again, OECD says
article:
(Sept 23): Inflation around the world will be faster than forecast in 2027, an outlook that necessitates more tightening from the US to Australia, the OECD said.

In a report released on Wednesday, the Paris-based club of rich countries raised projections compared with June for consumer-price growth in every Group-of-20 economy apart from China and Saudi Arabia. Monetary policy across the globe may have to respond, its officials added.

“Faced with renewed energy price shocks and stronger-than-expected demand pressures, and at a time when inflation is already above target in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained,” the OECD said in its report.

The analysis underscores how the economic impact of the Middle East war unleashed by US President Donald Trump is now set to endure into the second half of his term in office.

The OECD’s assessment follows a round of tightening this month, with the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan all raising interest rates within little more than a week of each other.

See also: Hong Kong’s Paul Chan rejects ‘race to bottom’ with Singapore

The organisation’s officials reckon more such action is in the offing, while suggesting it won’t match the aggressive policy moves seen in the wake of the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

It predicts one more hike this year by the Fed, “further modest increases” in the euro area, Australia and South Korea, and “additional policy rate increases” in Japan. By contrast, the OECD says that the Bank of England (BOE) and the Bank of Canada will keep rates steady for now.

That jars slightly with the views of investors. Money markets are almost evenly split on whether the Fed, ECB and BOE will deliver one or two more hikes by the end of this year. However, traders are more certain that the BOJ will move just once more by then, and they also favour the BOC to raise rates by a quarter point in that period.

See also: Asia to face sustained inflation pressure into 2027, ADB warns

The path of global growth is roughly unchanged compared with June, according to the OECD. Standing out from modest adjustments to its forecasts are downgrades in the outlooks for Canada, which faces a trade war with the US, and France, where a period of political instability looms.

“Global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved,” the OECD said. “Continued changes in trade policies, both tariffs and export restrictions, add to policy uncertainty and contribute to supply disruptions.”

The report also covered a range of risks bearing down on the world. Officials repeated longstanding calls for countries to repair public finances, highlighting how recent increases in bond yields “underline more than ever” the need to keep spending under control.

The OECD touched on the dangers of artificial intelligence too, observing that the technology could boost growth and productivity, but that it brings threats too.

“There is a risk that AI investment returns disappoint or take longer to materialise”, while “mounting security concerns related to AI could also slow the development of the technology or its adoption”, it said.

Leverage and complex financing are another worry, and returns may fall short.

“Disappointing earnings growth could materially slow investment in the sector, transmitting to other associated industries such as engineering and construction, and result in deteriorating valuations in financial markets,” the OECD said.

title: SIA Engineering and Rolls Royce JV SAESL eyes growth as MRO market expands to US$120 bil
article:
As the global maintenance, repair and operations (MRO) market is forecasted to increase to more than US$120 ($153) billion by 2030 from the current US$101 billion1, Singapore Aero Engine Services (SAESL), a joint venture between Mainboard-listed SIA Engineering and Rolls Royce, says that it is positioning itself for growth by developing human capital and advancing “next-generation” MRO technologies in Singapore, which currently accounts for 20% of global engine MRO output.

To this end, SAESL, which is the world's largest Rolls-Royce Trent engine MRO provider, has signed four Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), Republic Polytechnic (RP), Temasek Polytechnic (TP) and the A*STAR Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Centre (A*STAR ARTC).

According to a Sept 23 announcement, SAESL along with ITE, RP and TP, will create “meaningful pathways” towards aerospace and MRO careers for Singapore’s young talent through training modules, internships, traineeships, work-study programmes and hands-on industry experience. Coupled with Singapore accounting for 20% of global engine MRO output,

"Singapore's aerospace industry will continue to depend on a strong pipeline of skilled local talent and continued development of advanced technologies,” says SAESL CEO Chris Pattinson. “Through these partnerships, we are creating more opportunities for young talent to gain direct experience in aerospace MRO and build meaningful long-term careers in the sector.”

Meanwhile, SAESL’s collaboration with the A*STAR ARTC will focus on the development and deployment of advanced technologies including AI-native and autonomous inspection, assembly and disassembly solutions. This includes supporting local SMEs in adopting and industrialising advanced manufacturing technologies, helping build local capabilities across Singapore’s aerospace ecosystem.
